cards.q: In a reflex arc, what does the receptor do?
cards.a: It detects the stimulus and converts it into an electrical signal.
options: It produces the response, such as a contraction or a secretion
It decides which motor neurons should be activated and how strongly
It detects the stimulus and converts it into an electrical signal
It carries the command from the spinal cord out to the effector muscle
cards.explanation: The receptor is the first element of the arc: it transduces a stimulus such as stretch, heat, or pressure into a receptor potential that can trigger action potentials in the sensory neuron. Carrying the command outward is the job of the motor neuron. Deciding which motor neurons fire is the job of the integrating center in the central nervous system. Producing the response is the job of the effector, the muscle or gland at the end of the arc.

cards.q: Which component of a reflex arc carries information from the receptor into the central nervous system?
cards.a: The sensory neuron.
options: The interneuron in the spinal gray matter
The sensory neuron
The motor neuron
The effector organ
cards.explanation: The sensory, or afferent, neuron conducts the signal from the receptor into the spinal cord through the dorsal root. The motor neuron runs the other direction, out of the cord toward the effector. The interneuron lies entirely inside the central nervous system and never reaches the receptor. The effector is the muscle or gland that acts at the end of the arc, not a conducting element.

cards.q: For a spinal reflex, where is the integrating center?
cards.a: The gray matter of the spinal cord.
options: The gray matter of the spinal cord
The white matter columns of the spinal cord
The dorsal root ganglion
The primary motor cortex
cards.explanation: Integration means synapsing, and the synapses of a spinal reflex are made in the gray matter of the cord, where sensory terminals, interneurons, and motor neuron cell bodies meet. The dorsal root ganglion holds sensory cell bodies but contains no synapses. The motor cortex integrates voluntary movement, not spinal reflexes, which is why a reflex survives when the cord is cut off from the brain. White matter is myelinated axon tracts passing through, with no synapses.

cards.q: What counts as the effector in a reflex arc?
cards.a: A muscle or a gland.
options: An interneuron pool in the gray matter
A sensory receptor ending
A neuron in the dorsal root ganglion
A muscle or a gland
cards.explanation: The effector is whatever carries out the response, and only muscle and gland tissue can do that. A receptor ending starts the arc rather than ending it. A dorsal root ganglion neuron is the sensory limb. An interneuron pool is part of the integrating center, and it acts on motor neurons rather than producing the response itself.

cards.q: What makes a reflex monosynaptic?
cards.a: The sensory neuron synapses directly on the motor neuron.
options: The pathway uses exactly one sensory neuron
There is a single synapse at the neuromuscular junction
Only one muscle takes part in the response
The sensory neuron synapses directly on the motor neuron
cards.explanation: Monosynaptic counts synapses inside the central nervous system, and there is exactly one: sensory terminal onto motor neuron, with no interneuron between them. The number of sensory neurons is not what is being counted, since many Ia fibers converge on the same motor pool in a monosynaptic reflex. The number of muscles is also not the criterion. The neuromuscular junction is present in every reflex, monosynaptic or not, so it cannot distinguish them.

cards.q: What defines a polysynaptic reflex?
cards.a: At least one interneuron lies between the sensory and motor neurons.
options: The motor neuron fires more than one action potential in a row
More than one muscle contracts during the reflex response
At least one interneuron lies between the sensory and motor neurons
The sensory neuron branches into several different spinal segments
cards.explanation: Polysynaptic means two or more central synapses, which requires at least one interneuron inserted into the pathway. Branching of an afferent into several segments happens in monosynaptic reflexes too and does not add a synapse in series. Multiple muscles contracting is a common consequence of interneurons but is not the definition. Repeated firing of the motor neuron changes the strength of the response, not the number of synapses in the arc.

cards.q: Which reflex is the standard example of a monosynaptic reflex?
cards.a: The patellar stretch reflex.
options: The pupillary light reflex
The patellar stretch reflex
The flexor withdrawal reflex
The crossed extensor reflex
cards.explanation: In the patellar reflex the Ia afferent from the quadriceps spindle synapses directly on the alpha motor neurons of that same muscle, giving one central synapse and a very short latency. The flexor withdrawal reflex runs through chains of interneurons across several segments. The crossed extensor reflex adds interneurons that cross the midline. The pupillary light reflex passes through several brainstem nuclei, making it strongly polysynaptic.

cards.q: Where are the cell bodies of the somatic motor neurons of a spinal reflex arc?
cards.a: In the ventral horn of the spinal cord gray matter.
options: In the ventral horn of the spinal cord gray matter
In the dorsal horn of the spinal cord gray matter
In the lateral white column of the spinal cord
In the dorsal root ganglion
cards.explanation: Somatic motor neurons have their cell bodies in the ventral horn and send axons out through the ventral root to skeletal muscle. The dorsal root ganglion holds sensory cell bodies instead. The dorsal horn receives incoming sensory terminals and holds interneurons, not somatic motor neurons. White matter contains axons in transit and no neuronal cell bodies at all.

cards.q: One reflex in a limb has a latency of about 25 ms and another in the same limb has a latency of about 80 ms. What best explains the difference?
cards.a: The slower reflex has additional synapses in its central pathway.
options: The slower reflex acts on a stronger and larger effector muscle
The faster reflex uses unmyelinated afferent fibers only
The slower reflex uses a shorter peripheral nerve pathway
The slower reflex has additional synapses in its central pathway
cards.explanation: Each central synapse costs roughly half a millisecond to a millisecond, and a polysynaptic pathway also uses smaller, slower afferents, so latency climbs well above the monosynaptic value. A shorter nerve path would make a reflex faster, not slower. Unmyelinated fibers conduct slowly, so they would belong to the slower reflex rather than the faster one. Effector strength changes the size of the response, not the delay before it begins.

cards.q: The dorsal root of a spinal nerve is cut. What happens to a reflex whose arc runs through that segment?
cards.a: The reflex is lost because the sensory limb is interrupted.
options: The reflex is exaggerated because inhibition has been removed
The reflex is lost because the sensory limb is interrupted
The reflex is lost because the motor limb is interrupted
The reflex is normal because the interneurons are intact
cards.explanation: The dorsal root carries afferent axons into the cord, so cutting it means the stimulus never reaches the integrating center and the arc cannot be completed. The motor limb leaves through the ventral root and is untouched, which is why the muscle can still be activated voluntarily. Intact interneurons cannot help when nothing arrives to excite them. Removing input removes excitation, so exaggeration is the opposite of what happens.

cards.q: The ventral root of a spinal nerve is cut. What is the expected pattern of findings in the region it supplies?
cards.a: Sensation is preserved but the reflex response is absent.
options: Sensation is preserved but the reflex response is absent
Both sensation and the reflex response are lost
Sensation is lost but the reflex response is preserved
Both sensation and the reflex response are preserved
cards.explanation: The ventral root carries motor axons out, so cutting it removes the output limb while leaving the afferents in the dorsal root intact: the stimulus is still felt, but no contraction follows. Losing sensation while keeping the reflex is impossible, since the same afferents serve both. Preserving both would require an intact motor limb. Losing both is what a cut spinal nerve distal to the union of the two roots would produce, not a ventral root lesion alone.

cards.q: A patient feels the tendon tap normally, and the muscle contracts when stimulated directly with an electrode, but no reflex contraction occurs. Which component is most likely at fault?
cards.a: The alpha motor neuron or its synapse in the cord.
options: The extrafusal muscle fibers themselves
The sensory neuron running in the dorsal root
The alpha motor neuron or its synapse in the cord
The stretch receptor inside the muscle spindle
cards.explanation: Feeling the tap shows the receptor and afferent are working, and a muscle that contracts to direct stimulation shows the muscle itself is healthy, which leaves the efferent limb and its central synapse as the failure point. The receptor and the sensory neuron are cleared by the preserved sensation. The muscle fibers are cleared by the response to direct stimulation. Testing the limbs of the arc one at a time this way is how a reflex deficit gets localized.

cards.q: An autonomic reflex such as the baroreceptor reflex differs from a somatic reflex mainly in which component?
cards.a: The effector, which is cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, or gland.
options: The receptor, which produces no receptor potential
The sensory neuron, which conducts without action potentials
The integrating center, which must be the cerebral cortex
The effector, which is cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, or gland
cards.explanation: Autonomic and somatic reflexes share the same general plan, and the clearest difference is the effector: autonomic output goes to cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, and glands rather than to skeletal muscle. Autonomic receptors transduce stimuli into receptor potentials just as somatic ones do. The integrating center for the baroreceptor reflex is in the medulla, not the cortex. Autonomic afferents conduct action potentials like any other sensory neuron.

cards.q: A spinal cord is transected at T4. Weeks later, a tap on the patellar tendon still produces a knee jerk. Why?
cards.a: The whole arc for that reflex lies below the level of the transection.
options: The brain still reaches the muscle through the sympathetic chain
The whole arc for that reflex lies below the level of the transection
The muscle generates the contraction on its own without neurons
The signal reroutes around the transection through the dorsal columns
cards.explanation: The patellar reflex is integrated in the L2 to L4 segments, all of which sit below T4 and remain connected to the leg, so the arc is intact even with no communication with the brain. The dorsal columns are ascending sensory tracts and are cut by the same transection, so they cannot serve as a detour. The sympathetic chain does not innervate skeletal muscle. Skeletal muscle cannot generate its own contraction without motor neuron input.

cards.q: Which change to a reflex arc would slow the reflex the most?
cards.a: Demyelination of the afferent axons.
options: Increasing the strength of the stimulus
Warming the nerve by 1 C
Demyelination of the afferent axons
Insertion of one additional interneuron in the pathway
cards.explanation: Myelin is what makes saltatory conduction fast, so losing it can drop conduction velocity from tens of meters per second to a few, adding tens of milliseconds over a limb length. One extra interneuron adds only about half a millisecond to a millisecond of synaptic delay. Warming a nerve slightly speeds conduction rather than slowing it. A stronger stimulus recruits more fibers and can shorten latency a little, but it does not slow the reflex.

cards.q: A patient has no knee jerk on the right, normal touch sensation over the right thigh, and full strength when asked to extend the right knee. Where is the lesion most likely to be?
cards.a: In the Ia afferent fibers from the quadriceps muscle spindles.
options: In the Ia afferent fibers from the quadriceps muscle spindles
In the alpha motor neurons of the right ventral horn of the cord
In the right corticospinal tract in the spinal cord
In the extrafusal fibers of the right quadriceps
cards.explanation: Full voluntary strength clears the alpha motor neurons and the muscle, and normal touch clears the cutaneous afferents, so the missing piece must be the specific afferent that starts the stretch reflex, the Ia fiber from the spindle. Alpha motor neuron damage would also weaken voluntary extension. Damaged extrafusal fibers would weaken the muscle as well. A corticospinal lesion causes weakness with brisker, not absent, reflexes, since it removes descending inhibition of the arc.

cards.q: A local anesthetic is applied to a mixed nerve and blocks the largest myelinated fibers first. Which is lost earlier, the stretch reflex or the sensation of sharp pain?
cards.a: The stretch reflex, because its Ia afferents are the largest fibers present.
options: Both at the same time, because all fibers in a nerve are blocked together
The stretch reflex, because its Ia afferents are the largest fibers present
Neither, because anesthetics act only at the neuromuscular junction
Sharp pain, because pain fibers are the most sensitive to local anesthetics
cards.explanation: Ia spindle afferents are the largest diameter fibers in a peripheral nerve, so a block that works from largest to smallest silences them before it reaches the small fibers, and the tendon jerk disappears while pain is still felt. Sharp pain travels on small myelinated fibers, which are blocked later under this ordering. Fibers in a nerve are blocked in size order, not all at once. Local anesthetics block voltage gated Na+ channels along axons, not just at the junction.

cards.q: A toxin selectively blocks inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord. Predict the effect on the stretch reflex and on the antagonist muscle.
cards.a: The stretch reflex is exaggerated and the antagonist no longer relaxes, so both contract.
options: Both the stretch reflex and the antagonist response disappear, since the arc is interrupted
Only the antagonist is exaggerated and the stretched muscle falls silent
The stretch reflex disappears while the antagonist relaxes normally
The stretch reflex is exaggerated and the antagonist no longer relaxes, so both contract
cards.explanation: The excitatory monosynaptic limb is untouched, so the stretched muscle still contracts, and removing inhibitory interneurons both releases the motor pool from restraint and abolishes reciprocal inhibition, so the antagonist contracts along with it. The arc itself is not interrupted, so the reflex cannot vanish. The stretched muscle is driven by a direct excitatory synapse that needs no interneuron, so it cannot fall silent from this block. Blocking inhibition never selectively silences an excitatory pathway.

cards.q: A reflex arc has an afferent path of 0.8 m conducting at 80 m/s, an efferent path of 0.8 m conducting at 80 m/s, and one central synapse costing about 0.5 ms. Roughly how long is the delay from stimulus to the arrival of the signal at the muscle?
cards.a: About 21 ms.
options: About 21 ms
About 41 ms
About 2 ms
About 11 ms
cards.explanation: Each 0.8 m leg takes 0.8 divided by 80, which is 0.01 s or 10 ms, so the two legs total 20 ms, and adding the 0.5 ms synaptic delay gives about 21 ms. About 11 ms counts only one leg of the trip. About 41 ms would double the true conduction distance. About 2 ms is off by a factor of ten and would require conduction distances of centimeters rather than most of a limb.

cards.q: Which fibers inside a muscle spindle are wrapped by its sensory endings?
cards.a: Intrafusal muscle fibers.
options: Capsules of the Golgi tendon organs
Collagen bundles of the tendon
Intrafusal muscle fibers
Extrafusal muscle fibers
cards.explanation: A spindle is a capsule containing a few small intrafusal fibers, and the sensory ending coils around their noncontractile middle so that stretching the middle deforms the ending. Extrafusal fibers are the ordinary force generating fibers outside the capsule. Tendon collagen is where Golgi tendon organs sit, not spindles. Golgi tendon organ capsules are a separate receptor entirely, located in the tendon.

cards.q: How is the muscle spindle arranged relative to the force generating muscle fibers?
cards.a: In parallel with the extrafusal fibers.
options: In series with the extrafusal fibers
Outside the muscle in the joint capsule
In parallel with the extrafusal fibers
In series with the tendon at the muscle insertion
cards.explanation: Because the spindle lies side by side with the extrafusal fibers, stretching the whole muscle stretches the spindle too, and shortening the muscle unloads it. A receptor in series with the fibers would be loaded by the force those fibers generate, which is exactly how the Golgi tendon organ is arranged. Sitting in series at the insertion describes the tendon organ again. Joint capsule receptors report joint angle and are a different class of receptor.

cards.q: Which afferent fiber carries the primary sensory signal from the muscle spindle?
cards.a: The group Ia afferent.
options: The group Ia afferent
The group III afferent
The group Ib afferent
The group IV afferent
cards.explanation: The primary annulospiral ending of the spindle sends its signal on a group Ia fiber, the largest and fastest afferent, which is why the stretch reflex has such a short latency. Group Ib fibers come from Golgi tendon organs and report tension. Group III and group IV fibers are small and carry pain and metabolic information from muscle. Group II fibers, not listed as the key here, carry the secondary spindle ending.

cards.q: Which motor neurons innervate the contractile ends of the intrafusal fibers?
cards.a: Gamma motor neurons.
options: Ib inhibitory interneurons
Gamma motor neurons
Postganglionic sympathetic neurons
Alpha motor neurons
cards.explanation: Gamma motor neurons supply only the intrafusal fibers, and by contracting their ends they stretch the sensory middle and reset spindle sensitivity. Alpha motor neurons supply the extrafusal fibers that generate force. Ib inhibitory interneurons act inside the cord on motor neurons and never leave the central nervous system. Sympathetic neurons innervate smooth muscle and glands, not skeletal muscle fibers of any kind.

cards.q: Which motor neurons innervate the extrafusal fibers that generate the muscle force?
cards.a: Alpha motor neurons.
options: Renshaw interneurons
Group II afferent neurons
Gamma motor neurons
Alpha motor neurons
cards.explanation: Alpha motor neurons are the final common path to the extrafusal fibers, and their firing is what produces the contraction you can see. Gamma motor neurons go to the intrafusal fibers within the spindle and produce no useful force. Renshaw cells are inhibitory interneurons in the cord that feed back onto motor neurons. Group II fibers are afferents carrying information in, not motor fibers carrying commands out.

cards.q: What is the adequate stimulus for the muscle spindle?
cards.a: A change in muscle length.
options: A change in the temperature of the muscle
A change in muscle length
A change in pressure inside the joint capsule
A change in muscle tension
cards.explanation: Because the spindle lies in parallel with the working fibers, what deforms its sensory ending is stretch, so it reports length and the rate at which length is changing. Tension is the stimulus for the Golgi tendon organ, which sits in series in the tendon. Joint capsule pressure is sensed by joint receptors. Temperature is sensed by thermoreceptors, which have no role in the stretch reflex.

cards.q: In the stretch reflex, what happens to the muscle that was stretched?
cards.a: It contracts.
options: It contracts
It relaxes
It is inhibited while its antagonist contracts
It stays unchanged until a command arrives from the brain
cards.explanation: Ia firing from the stretched spindle excites the alpha motor neurons of that same muscle directly, so the muscle contracts and resists the stretch, which is what keeps a limb position stable. Relaxation is the response of a muscle whose Golgi tendon organs are strongly loaded, not the response to stretch. Inhibition of the stretched muscle while the antagonist contracts is the reverse of the actual wiring. No brain command is needed, since the arc is complete within the cord.

cards.q: What is reciprocal inhibition in the stretch reflex?
cards.a: An inhibitory interneuron reduces firing of the motor neurons to the antagonist muscle.
options: An inhibitory interneuron reduces firing of the motor neurons to the stretched muscle
The spindle stops firing once the muscle has shortened
An inhibitory interneuron reduces firing of the motor neurons to the antagonist muscle
The Golgi tendon organ shuts down the muscle at high force
cards.explanation: A branch of the Ia afferent excites an inhibitory interneuron that suppresses the motor pool of the opposing muscle, so the antagonist relaxes and does not fight the reflex contraction. Inhibiting the stretched muscle itself would cancel the reflex, which is the opposite of what happens. Spindle unloading during shortening is a change in receptor firing, not an inhibitory circuit. Shutdown at high force is autogenic inhibition through Ib fibers, a different reflex.

cards.q: The patellar tendon is tapped. Predict what the quadriceps and the hamstrings do.
cards.a: The quadriceps contracts and the hamstrings relax.
options: Both contract together and stiffen the knee
Both relax and the leg drops
The hamstrings contract and the quadriceps relax
The quadriceps contracts and the hamstrings relax
cards.explanation: The tap stretches the quadriceps spindles, and their Ia fibers excite quadriceps motor neurons directly while inhibiting the hamstring motor neurons through an inhibitory interneuron, so the knee extends smoothly. Contraction of the hamstrings would be the reflex of a muscle that had been stretched, which the tap did not do. Co-contraction would occur only if reciprocal inhibition were blocked. Both muscles relaxing describes loss of the reflex, not the normal response.

cards.q: A muscle is allowed to shorten quickly while gamma motor neurons stay silent. What happens to Ia firing from the spindle?
cards.a: It falls, because the spindle is unloaded.
options: It falls, because the spindle is unloaded
It rises briefly and then stops because the receptor fatigues
It rises, because the shortening compresses the spindle
It is unchanged, because the spindle senses tension rather than length
cards.explanation: A spindle in parallel with shortening fibers goes slack, the sensory middle is no longer stretched, and firing drops or stops. Compression is not the stimulus for the spindle, so shortening cannot excite it that way. The spindle reports length, not tension, so an unchanged rate would only be expected of a tension receptor. Fatigue is not the issue here, since the same spindle fires again as soon as the muscle is stretched or gamma drive is restored.

cards.q: What does gamma coactivation accomplish during a voluntary contraction?
cards.a: It shortens the spindle with the muscle so it keeps reporting length changes.
options: It silences the spindle so that the reflex cannot oppose the movement
It adds directly to the force that the whole muscle produces
It shortens the spindle with the muscle so it keeps reporting length changes
It converts the spindle into a detector of tension rather than of length
cards.explanation: Firing gamma neurons together with alpha neurons takes up the slack in the intrafusal fibers, so the spindle stays taut and can still sense an unexpected stretch during a shortening contraction. Intrafusal fibers are far too few and too small to add meaningful force. Silencing the spindle is what happens without gamma coactivation, which is the problem it solves. Nothing about gamma drive changes what the receptor measures, which remains length.

cards.q: How many synapses in the spinal cord does reciprocal inhibition of the antagonist require?
cards.a: At least two, because an inhibitory interneuron is inserted.
options: One, the same synapse the agonist uses
At least two, because an inhibitory interneuron is inserted
None, because the inhibition occurs at the muscle
Three or more, because the signal must cross to the other side
cards.explanation: The Ia fiber synapses on an inhibitory interneuron, which in turn synapses on the antagonist motor neuron, so this limb of the reflex is polysynaptic even though the agonist limb is monosynaptic. A single synapse would deliver excitation, since Ia afferents are excitatory. Inhibition of skeletal muscle never occurs at the muscle itself, only in the cord. The pathway stays on the same side, so no midline crossing is involved.

cards.q: Which spindle ending responds best to the rate at which a muscle is being stretched?
cards.a: The primary ending on its group Ia fiber.
options: The tendon organ on its group Ib fiber
The free nerve ending in the muscle belly
The secondary ending on its group II fiber
The primary ending on its group Ia fiber
cards.explanation: The primary ending is strongly dynamic: it fires a burst proportional to how fast the muscle is lengthening, which is why a brisk tap works so much better than a slow pull. The secondary ending is mainly static and reports steady length. The tendon organ reports force and is not part of the spindle. Free nerve endings in muscle carry pain and metabolic signals, not length information.

cards.q: A muscle is stretched steadily and then held at the new length. What Ia firing pattern is expected?
cards.a: A large burst during the stretch, then a lower steady rate at the new length.
options: A steady rate during the stretch that increases when the length is held
A large burst during the stretch, then a lower steady rate at the new length
A burst during the stretch, then complete silence at the new length
No firing during the stretch, then a burst once the length is held
cards.explanation: The dynamic response tracks the velocity of stretch, so firing peaks while the length is changing, and the static response then holds a lower rate that encodes the new length. Firing cannot wait for the movement to stop, since velocity is highest during the stretch itself. A rate that rises after the stretch ends would mean velocity sensitivity in reverse. Complete silence at the new length would erase the position information the spindle exists to provide.

cards.q: Why does the stretch reflex help keep a limb steady when an unexpected load is added?
cards.a: The load stretches the muscle, and the reflex contraction opposes it.
options: The load raises tension, and the spindle responds by inhibiting the muscle
The load shortens the muscle, and the reflex then relaxes it further
The load stretches the muscle, and the reflex contraction opposes it
The load excites the Golgi tendon organ, which then excites the muscle
cards.explanation: An added load lengthens the muscle a little, the spindles fire, and the resulting contraction pulls the limb back toward its original position, forming a negative feedback loop for length. A load lengthens rather than shortens the muscle, so the second option starts from the wrong direction. The spindle is excitatory to its own muscle, not inhibitory, and it responds to length rather than tension. The Golgi tendon organ does respond to tension, but its reflex effect on its own muscle is inhibition.

cards.q: Gamma motor neurons to a muscle are blocked while its alpha motor neurons are left intact. Predict the tendon jerk and the spindle behavior during a voluntary contraction.
cards.a: The tendon jerk is weaker than normal and the spindle falls silent as the muscle shortens.
options: The tendon jerk is exaggerated and the spindle fires faster as the muscle shortens further
The tendon jerk is normal, because gamma motor neurons act only on the antagonist
The tendon jerk is abolished and voluntary contraction becomes impossible too
The tendon jerk is weaker than normal and the spindle falls silent as the muscle shortens
cards.explanation: Without gamma drive the intrafusal fibers stay slack, so the resting sensitivity of the spindle drops and the tap produces a smaller Ia burst and a weaker jerk, and during shortening the unloaded spindle stops firing altogether. Exaggeration would require more spindle sensitivity, not less. Voluntary contraction is unaffected because alpha motor neurons still reach the extrafusal fibers. Gamma neurons supply the spindles of their own muscle, not the antagonist.

cards.q: A large fiber sensory neuropathy destroys Ia afferents while sparing small fibers and all motor fibers. What pattern of findings is expected?
cards.a: Tendon jerks are lost and position sense is impaired, while strength is preserved.
options: Tendon jerks are lost and position sense is impaired, while strength is preserved
Pain sensation is lost first and the tendon jerks become exaggerated over time
Strength is lost while tendon jerks and position sense remain entirely normal
Tendon jerks are exaggerated because descending inhibition has been removed
cards.explanation: Ia fibers are both the afferent limb of the tendon jerk and a major source of proprioceptive information, so losing them abolishes the jerk and degrades position sense while leaving intact motor axons and intact small pain fibers. Strength depends on motor fibers, which are spared. Pain travels on small fibers, which this neuropathy does not touch. Exaggerated reflexes come from removing descending inhibition in the cord, not from cutting the afferent limb, which can only weaken the reflex.

cards.q: A standing person sways slightly forward, which stretches the calf muscles. Trace what happens next.
cards.a: Ia firing rises, the calf muscles contract, and the body is pulled back toward upright.
options: Ib firing rises, the calf muscles are inhibited, and the person tips further forward
Ia firing rises, the calf muscles contract, and the body is pulled back toward upright
Ia firing rises, the shin muscles contract, and the forward sway increases
Ia firing falls, the calf muscles relax, and the forward sway continues
cards.explanation: Forward sway lengthens the calf, spindles fire, and the monosynaptic reflex contracts the same stretched muscle, which plantar flexes the ankle and restores the upright position without any conscious effort. Falling Ia firing would require the muscle to shorten, which forward sway does not do. Ib driven inhibition needs a large rise in tension, and it would worsen the sway rather than correct it. Contracting the shin muscles is what reciprocal inhibition prevents, since those are the antagonists here.

cards.q: The inhibitory interneuron that mediates reciprocal inhibition at a joint is blocked, but the monosynaptic connection is intact. Predict the response to a tendon tap.
cards.a: The tapped muscle contracts, but its antagonist contracts too, so the joint stiffens.
options: Only the antagonist contracts, so the joint moves in the opposite direction
Neither muscle contracts, because the reflex arc has been broken at its only synapse
The tapped muscle contracts, but its antagonist contracts too, so the joint stiffens
The tapped muscle relaxes while its antagonist contracts instead
cards.explanation: The direct Ia to alpha synapse is untouched, so the stretched muscle contracts on schedule, but with reciprocal inhibition gone the antagonist is no longer silenced and co-contracts, producing stiffness instead of a clean movement. The arc itself is not broken, so a complete loss of response is not possible. The antagonist has no excitatory drive of its own here, so it cannot act alone. Relaxation of the tapped muscle would require inhibiting the very pool the Ia fiber excites.

cards.q: Where is the Golgi tendon organ located?
cards.a: In the tendon, in series with the muscle fibers.
options: In the connective tissue sheath around each fascicle
In the joint capsule next to the ligament
In the muscle belly, in parallel with the muscle fibers
In the tendon, in series with the muscle fibers
cards.explanation: The tendon organ sits at the junction of muscle and tendon so that all the force the fibers generate passes directly through it, which makes it a force meter. A receptor in parallel in the muscle belly is the spindle, and it measures length instead. Joint capsule receptors report joint angle and take no part in this reflex. A receptor inside the fascicle sheath would not be loaded by whole muscle force.

cards.q: Which afferent fiber carries the signal from the Golgi tendon organ?
cards.a: The group Ib afferent.
options: The group Ib afferent
The group IV afferent
The group Ia afferent
The group II afferent
cards.explanation: Group Ib fibers are large and fast, matching the rapid protective role of the tendon organ reflex. Group Ia fibers carry the primary spindle signal about length and its rate of change. Group II fibers carry the secondary spindle ending, also a length signal. Group IV fibers are small unmyelinated fibers carrying pain and metabolic information from muscle.

cards.q: What is the adequate stimulus for the Golgi tendon organ?
cards.a: Tension developed in the tendon.
options: Length of the muscle belly
Temperature within the tendon
Tension developed in the tendon
Rate of change of the joint angle
cards.explanation: Because the tendon organ is in series with the muscle fibers, whatever force they produce squeezes its collagen bundles onto the nerve endings, so its firing rate tracks tension. Muscle length is what the spindle measures. Joint angle and its rate of change are reported by joint receptors and, indirectly, by spindles. Temperature has no role in this receptor.

cards.q: What is the reflex response to strong Golgi tendon organ firing?
cards.a: Inhibition of the motor neurons supplying that same muscle.
options: Inhibition of the motor neurons supplying that same muscle
Excitation of the gamma motor neurons of that same muscle
Inhibition of the motor neurons supplying the antagonist
Excitation of the motor neurons supplying that same muscle
cards.explanation: Ib input drives an inhibitory interneuron onto the motor pool of its own muscle, so rising tension reduces the drive that created it, a negative feedback loop for force. Excitation of the same muscle is the effect of spindle input, not tendon organ input. The antagonist is excited rather than inhibited by this reflex. Gamma motor neurons are not the target of the Ib pathway.

cards.q: How many synapses does the Golgi tendon organ reflex use inside the spinal cord before reaching the alpha motor neuron?
cards.a: At least two, because an inhibitory interneuron is inserted.
options: One, a direct inhibitory synapse
None, because the effect occurs at the neuromuscular junction
One, a direct excitatory synapse
At least two, because an inhibitory interneuron is inserted
cards.explanation: Ib afferents are excitatory, like all primary afferents, so producing inhibition requires them to excite an inhibitory interneuron first, making the pathway polysynaptic. A single excitatory synapse would produce contraction rather than relaxation. Primary afferents do not make inhibitory synapses directly, so a one synapse inhibitory arc does not exist here. Inhibition of skeletal muscle never happens at the neuromuscular junction, which is always excitatory.

cards.q: What happens to the antagonist muscle when a Golgi tendon organ fires strongly?
cards.a: It is excited.
options: It is unaffected
It is excited
It is inhibited
It is disconnected from its motor neurons
cards.explanation: The Ib pathway inhibits its own muscle and excites the antagonist, so the joint yields in the opposite direction and the dangerous force is relieved. Inhibiting the antagonist as well would leave the joint with no active control. Leaving the antagonist unaffected would waste the chance to unload the tendon. Motor neurons are never physically disconnected by a reflex, only excited or inhibited.

cards.q: Which of these receptors has its own motor innervation?
cards.a: The muscle spindle, through gamma motor neurons.
options: Both receptors receive motor innervation
Neither receptor receives motor innervation
The muscle spindle, through gamma motor neurons
The Golgi tendon organ, through Ib motor fibers
cards.explanation: Only the spindle contains contractile tissue, the ends of the intrafusal fibers, and gamma motor neurons adjust their length to set the sensitivity of the receptor. Group Ib is an afferent designation, so there is no such thing as a Ib motor fiber. The tendon organ is a purely passive collagen and nerve ending structure with no way to be reset centrally. Saying neither is innervated would leave the gamma system with nothing to do.

cards.q: What is the name for the reflex effect a Golgi tendon organ has on its own muscle?
cards.a: Autogenic inhibition.
options: Reciprocal inhibition
Autogenic inhibition
Presynaptic facilitation
Recurrent inhibition
cards.explanation: Autogenic means acting on the source, so the term captures a receptor inhibiting the very muscle whose tension excited it. Reciprocal inhibition is the suppression of the antagonist during a stretch reflex, a different target. Recurrent inhibition is the Renshaw cell loop, in which a motor neuron collateral inhibits the motor pool. Presynaptic facilitation describes an increase in transmitter release at a terminal and is not a reflex name.

cards.q: A muscle contracts hard isometrically against an immovable bar. Which receptor increases its firing the most?
cards.a: The Golgi tendon organ, because tension rises sharply.
options: The muscle spindle, because muscle length rises
Neither, because nothing moves
Both equally, because both receptors sense force
The Golgi tendon organ, because tension rises sharply
cards.explanation: An isometric contraction changes force without changing whole muscle length, which is exactly the condition that loads a series receptor and leaves a parallel one nearly unchanged. Muscle length does not rise during an isometric contraction, so the spindle has no reason to fire more. The absence of movement does not mean the absence of a stimulus, since tension is a stimulus. The two receptors sense different variables, so treating them as equal misses the whole contrast.

cards.q: A completely relaxed muscle is stretched passively. Which statement is correct?
cards.a: Both receptors are stimulated, but the spindle responds far more strongly.
options: Both receptors are stimulated, but the spindle responds far more strongly
Neither receptor responds until the muscle contracts voluntarily
Only the tendon organ responds, because stretching raises the tension
Only the spindle responds, because a tendon itself cannot be stretched
cards.explanation: Passive stretch lengthens the parallel spindle strongly and puts only a small passive tension on the series tendon organ, so both fire but the spindle dominates. Passive tension is real but small, so calling the tendon organ the only responder overstates it. Tendons do take up passive load, so the claim that they cannot be stretched is wrong. Both receptors work perfectly well in a relaxed muscle and need no voluntary command.

cards.q: Which receptor most directly helps hold grip force steady while carrying a heavy bag?
cards.a: The Golgi tendon organ, which monitors force.
options: The Golgi tendon organ, which monitors force
The muscle spindle, which monitors force
The Golgi tendon organ, which monitors length
The muscle spindle, which monitors joint angle
cards.explanation: Steady force is a force problem, and the tendon organ is the receptor whose firing is proportional to the tension the muscle is producing, so it supplies the feedback that a force controller needs. The spindle does not monitor force, so pairing it with force is the common mix up. Length is the spindle variable and does not belong to the tendon organ. Joint angle is reported by joint receptors and again is not what a spindle measures directly.

cards.q: A receptor lies in series with the muscle fibers and inhibits its own muscle when it fires. Which receptor is described?
cards.a: The Golgi tendon organ.
options: The nociceptor in the muscle belly
The joint capsule receptor
The muscle spindle
The Golgi tendon organ
cards.explanation: Series placement and autogenic inhibition are the two defining features of the tendon organ, and they belong together because a series receptor is the one loaded by force. A spindle is in parallel and excites its own muscle. A joint capsule receptor is outside the muscle entirely and reports position. A muscle nociceptor triggers withdrawal and pain responses and is not arranged in series to measure force.

cards.q: During a maximal lift the load suddenly feels as though it gives way and the muscle relaxes. Which reflex best explains this?
cards.a: Autogenic inhibition driven by Golgi tendon organs.
options: Reciprocal inhibition of the antagonist muscle
The stretch reflex driven by muscle spindles
Autogenic inhibition driven by Golgi tendon organs
The crossed extensor reflex
cards.explanation: At very high force the Ib input becomes strong enough to override the excitatory drive to the motor pool, and the muscle abruptly relaxes, unloading the tendon before it tears. The stretch reflex causes contraction, not sudden relaxation, so it cannot explain a give. Reciprocal inhibition acts on the opposing muscle and would not silence the one doing the lifting. The crossed extensor reflex involves the opposite limb and a painful stimulus.

cards.q: How should the latencies of the stretch reflex and the Golgi tendon organ reflex compare?
cards.a: The tendon organ reflex is slower because of its extra interneuron.
options: The stretch reflex is slower because it also inhibits the antagonist
The tendon organ reflex is slower because of its extra interneuron
The tendon organ reflex is faster because Ib fibers are larger than Ia fibers
They are identical because both use a single central synapse
cards.explanation: Ia and Ib fibers conduct at about the same speed, so the difference in latency comes from the number of central synapses, and the extra inhibitory interneuron in the Ib pathway adds delay. Ib fibers are not larger than Ia fibers, so that reasoning fails at the premise. Only the stretch reflex has a single central synapse, so the two cannot be identical. The reciprocal inhibition limb of the stretch reflex runs in parallel with the direct limb and does not delay the agonist contraction.

cards.q: A person lowers a heavy weight slowly, so the muscle is lengthening while generating high force. Predict the firing of the spindles and the tendon organs.
cards.a: Both fire strongly, since the muscle is stretched and under high tension at once.
options: Both fire strongly, since the muscle is stretched and under high tension at once
Neither fires, since the whole movement is under voluntary cortical control
Only the spindles fire, since tension falls while the muscle is lengthening
Only the tendon organs fire, since the length of the muscle is not changing
cards.explanation: An eccentric contraction is the one condition that maximizes both variables at once, lengthening the parallel spindles while forcing high tension through the series tendon organs. Tension is high, not falling, during a controlled lowering, so the spindle only answer misreads the mechanics. Length is clearly changing during a lowering movement, so the tendon organ only answer misreads it in the other direction. Voluntary control of a movement does not switch off proprioceptors, which report during voluntary and passive movement alike.

cards.q: The Ib inhibitory interneurons serving a muscle are blocked while everything else is intact. Predict what happens during a maximal voluntary contraction.
cards.a: Force continues to rise with no reflex braking, so tendon strain increases.
options: The stretch reflex disappears along with the reflex braking effect
Force drops immediately, because the muscle loses its excitatory drive
Force continues to rise with no reflex braking, so tendon strain increases
The antagonist contracts instead of relaxing during the whole effort
cards.explanation: Removing the inhibitory interneuron removes the negative feedback loop for force, so the motor pool is no longer restrained at high tension and the tendon carries more load than it normally would. Excitatory drive comes from descending commands and is untouched, so force cannot collapse. The stretch reflex uses a different, monosynaptic excitatory pathway and continues to work. The antagonist is controlled by other interneurons and is not switched on by this block.

cards.q: In a recording, afferent A fires briskly during passive stretch and goes silent during an active shortening contraction, while afferent B fires weakly during passive stretch and strongly during the active contraction. Identify the two afferents.
cards.a: A is a Ia spindle afferent and B is a Ib tendon organ afferent.
options: Both are Ib tendon organ afferents from different heads of the same muscle
A is a Ib tendon organ afferent and B is a Ia spindle afferent
Both are Ia spindle afferents from muscles on opposite sides of the joint
A is a Ia spindle afferent and B is a Ib tendon organ afferent
cards.explanation: Going silent during a shortening contraction is the signature of unloading a parallel receptor, and firing hardest when force is greatest is the signature of a series receptor, so A is the spindle and B is the tendon organ. Reversing the assignment would require a tension receptor to fall silent at high tension. Two spindles on opposite sides would both respond to length, and the antagonist spindle would be stretched rather than silent during shortening. Two tendon organs would both peak during the contraction, so their patterns would not differ this way.

cards.q: A therapist holds a steady stretch on a tight muscle for 30 seconds and the muscle gradually relaxes, whereas a quick stretch of the same muscle makes it tighten. What accounts for the difference?
cards.a: Sustained tension recruits Golgi tendon organs, whose inhibition outlasts a brief spindle response.
options: Sustained stretch recruits muscle spindles, whose excitation grows steadily the longer it is held
Sustained tension recruits Golgi tendon organs, whose inhibition outlasts a brief spindle response
Sustained stretch silences the Ib fibers, which removes all inhibition of the muscle
A fast stretch recruits Golgi tendon organs while a slow hold recruits the muscle spindles
cards.explanation: A quick stretch is a velocity stimulus that the dynamic spindle ending answers with a brief contraction, while a long hold keeps tension on the tendon and lets Ib driven autogenic inhibition dominate, so the muscle lets go. Spindle excitation adapts during a hold rather than growing. Sustained tension increases Ib firing rather than silencing it. The receptor assignments in the last option are reversed, since velocity is the spindle stimulus and force is the tendon organ stimulus.

cards.q: Which receptor starts the flexor withdrawal reflex?
cards.a: A nociceptor.
options: A Golgi tendon organ
A Pacinian corpuscle
A nociceptor
A muscle spindle
cards.explanation: Withdrawal is triggered by tissue damaging stimuli, and nociceptors are the free nerve endings that detect them. A muscle spindle detects stretch and starts the stretch reflex instead. A Golgi tendon organ detects tension and produces autogenic inhibition. A Pacinian corpuscle detects vibration and rapid pressure change, which does not by itself drive withdrawal.

cards.q: Is the flexor withdrawal reflex monosynaptic or polysynaptic?
cards.a: Polysynaptic.
options: Polysynaptic
Monosynaptic on the stimulated side and polysynaptic on the other side
It uses no synapse within the spinal cord
Monosynaptic
cards.explanation: Nociceptive afferents reach flexor motor neurons only through chains of interneurons, and those interneurons also spread the signal across several segments, so the arc is polysynaptic throughout. A monosynaptic arrangement is limited to the stretch reflex. There is no side of this reflex that is monosynaptic, since even the ipsilateral limb runs through interneurons. Every spinal reflex has at least one synapse in the cord, so a synapse free arc is not possible.

cards.q: In the flexor withdrawal reflex, which muscles contract on the stimulated side?
cards.a: The flexors.
options: Only the muscles acting at the joint nearest the stimulus
The flexors
The extensors
Both the flexors and the extensors
cards.explanation: Flexion pulls the limb away from the stimulus, so flexor motor neurons are excited while extensor motor neurons are inhibited. Contracting the extensors would push the limb toward the stimulus. Contracting both would lock the limb in place and prevent escape. Interneurons spread the response across several segments, so the response usually involves several joints rather than only the nearest one.

cards.q: What happens to the extensors on the stimulated side during a withdrawal reflex?
cards.a: They are inhibited.
options: They are excited
They contract after a short delay
They are unaffected by the reflex
They are inhibited
cards.explanation: Interneurons inhibit the extensor motor pool so the flexors can shorten the limb without opposition, the same reciprocal arrangement used in the stretch reflex. Exciting them would produce co-contraction and block the withdrawal. A delayed contraction of the extensors would return the limb toward the stimulus. Leaving them unaffected would leave resting extensor tone fighting the movement.

cards.q: In the crossed extensor reflex, what happens on the side opposite the painful stimulus?
cards.a: The extensors contract.
options: The flexors contract
The extensors contract
Nothing, because the reflex is confined to one side
Both the flexors and the extensors relax
cards.explanation: Commissural interneurons cross the cord and excite extensor motor neurons on the opposite side so that limb can stiffen and take the body weight. Contralateral flexion would lift both limbs at once and drop the person. Relaxing both muscle groups would leave the supporting limb unable to bear load. The whole point of this reflex is that it is not confined to one side.

cards.q: What is the functional purpose of the crossed extensor reflex?
cards.a: To support the body weight on the opposite limb while the stimulated limb withdraws.
options: To support the body weight on the opposite limb while the stimulated limb withdraws
To pull the opposite limb away from the painful stimulus as well
To slow the withdrawal so that the moving limb is not injured by the movement
To carry the pain signal upward to the cerebral cortex for awareness
cards.explanation: Lifting one leg suddenly shifts all the body weight to the other, and the crossed reflex extends that limb at the same instant so balance is preserved. Withdrawing both limbs would remove all support. Slowing the withdrawal would defeat its protective purpose and is not what the crossed pathway does. Carrying pain to the cortex is the job of the ascending spinothalamic pathway, a separate route.

cards.q: What allows a single withdrawal reflex to involve muscles at several joints?
cards.a: Divergence of interneurons across several spinal segments.
options: Convergence of many afferents onto a single motor neuron
Spread of the signal from muscle to muscle along the limb
Branching of one motor neuron to several different muscles
Divergence of interneurons across several spinal segments
cards.explanation: One nociceptive afferent excites interneurons that ascend and descend in the cord and distribute the signal to many motor pools, which is divergence. Convergence describes many inputs onto one cell and would narrow the response rather than widen it. A motor neuron innervates fibers within a single muscle, so it cannot branch across muscles. Skeletal muscle fibers do not pass excitation to neighboring muscles.

cards.q: What is afterdischarge in the withdrawal reflex?
cards.a: Continued motor neuron firing after the stimulus has stopped.
options: A second painful stimulus that follows shortly after the first
The inhibition of the flexors once withdrawal is complete
Continued motor neuron firing after the stimulus has stopped
The slow return of the limb to its original resting position
cards.explanation: Interneuron chains and reverberating loops keep delivering excitation to the motor pool for a period after the afferent volley ends, which is why a limb stays flexed after a brief stimulus. A second stimulus is an external event, not a property of the circuit. The passive return of the limb happens after the reflex ends and is not the discharge itself. Inhibition of the flexors is the opposite of continued flexor firing.

cards.q: A person standing barefoot steps on a tack with the right foot. Predict what the left leg does.
cards.a: The left leg extends to bear the body weight.
options: The left leg extends to bear the body weight
The left leg flexes so that both feet lift
The left leg does nothing until the person decides to shift
The left leg relaxes completely
cards.explanation: Crossed extensor output excites the contralateral extensors at the same time the right leg withdraws, so the left leg stiffens and supports the shifted weight. Flexing both legs would drop the person to the floor. Complete relaxation would collapse the supporting limb. The response is spinal and begins well before any voluntary decision can be made.

cards.q: Why does the flexor withdrawal reflex have a longer latency than the patellar reflex?
cards.a: It uses smaller, slower afferents and adds interneurons in the pathway.
options: It travels a longer distance within the peripheral nerve trunk
It uses smaller, slower afferents and adds interneurons in the pathway
Its effector muscles are larger and so take longer to contract fully
It must reach the cerebral cortex before any response can occur
cards.explanation: Nociceptive afferents are small and conduct slowly, and each interneuron in the chain adds synaptic delay, so both factors push the latency well above the monosynaptic value. Peripheral distances are similar for reflexes tested in the same limb. Muscle size affects the force and speed of the contraction, not the delay before it starts. The reflex is integrated in the cord, and cortical involvement is not required for the response.

cards.q: A stronger painful stimulus produces withdrawal at more joints than a weak one. What accounts for this?
cards.a: More interneurons are recruited, spreading excitation to more segments.
options: Muscle fibers generate more force from exactly the same motor command
Afferent fibers conduct faster when the stimulus applied is stronger
More interneurons are recruited, spreading excitation to more segments
Motor neurons produce larger action potentials with stronger input
cards.explanation: A stronger stimulus recruits more afferents and drives interneuron pools harder, so excitation spreads to motor pools further up and down the cord and more joints join the movement. Conduction velocity is a property of fiber diameter and myelination and does not change with stimulus strength. Action potentials are all or none, so they do not grow larger. Muscle force here rises because more motor units are recruited, which is a consequence of the spread rather than the cause of it.

cards.q: A hand touches a hot pan. Which muscles are activated first in the withdrawal response?
cards.a: The elbow flexors, which pull the hand away.
options: The elbow extensors, which push the hand away
The shoulder abductors acting alone
The flexors and extensors together, which hold the arm steady
The elbow flexors, which pull the hand away
cards.explanation: Withdrawal is a flexion pattern, and flexing the elbow is the fastest way to move the hand off the source of injury. Extending the elbow would drive the hand further into the pan. The shoulder often joins the movement, but it does so through the same spreading interneurons rather than acting on its own. Co-contraction would freeze the arm in contact with the heat.

cards.q: Which reflex depends on interneurons that cross to the opposite side of the spinal cord?
cards.a: The crossed extensor reflex.
options: The crossed extensor reflex
The Golgi tendon organ reflex
The patellar stretch reflex
The flexor withdrawal reflex
cards.explanation: Only the crossed extensor reflex sends its signal through commissural interneurons to motor pools on the other side of the body. The flexor withdrawal reflex is ipsilateral, even though it spans several segments. The stretch reflex acts on one muscle and its antagonist on the same side. The tendon organ reflex likewise stays within the same side of the cord.

cards.q: Withdrawal begins before the person consciously feels the pain. What does that show about the integrating center?
cards.a: Integration occurs in the cord, while conscious pain requires reaching the brain.
options: Integration occurs in the cortex, which acts before it becomes aware of the pain
The reflex bypasses synapses entirely, which is why it seems instantaneous
Integration occurs in the cord, while conscious pain requires reaching the brain
Pain fibers conduct faster than the motor fibers used by the reflex arc
cards.explanation: The reflex arc closes locally in the cord over a few tens of milliseconds, while the ascending pathway and cortical processing needed for awareness take considerably longer, so the movement leads the sensation. Cortical integration would add the very delay that the timing rules out. Comparing conduction speeds does not explain awareness, which depends on the number and length of the pathways involved. The withdrawal arc is polysynaptic, so it is not synapse free and not instantaneous.

cards.q: A person walking barefoot steps on broken glass with the left foot. Trace what the flexor withdrawal and crossed extensor reflexes do together.
cards.a: The left leg flexes and lifts while the right leg extends and takes the weight.
options: Both legs flex at once so that the person can lower to the ground safely
The left leg flexes and lifts while the right leg extends and takes the weight
The left leg extends to push off the glass while the right leg flexes
The left leg flexes and the right leg also flexes in order to shorten the stride
cards.explanation: Ipsilateral interneurons excite left flexors and inhibit left extensors, while commissural interneurons excite right extensors and inhibit right flexors, so escape and support happen in the same moment. Flexing both legs removes support and drops the body. Extending the injured leg would press the wound onto the glass. Flexing both legs also fails the balance requirement that the crossed pathway exists to meet.

cards.q: In a patient the commissural interneurons that cross the spinal cord are damaged while all ipsilateral circuits remain intact. Predict the response to a painful stimulus to one foot while the patient is standing.
cards.a: The stimulated leg withdraws but the other does not extend, so balance is lost.
options: Both legs extend, leaving the patient rigid
The stimulated leg extends and the other withdraws, reversing the pattern
Neither leg responds, because the whole reflex requires the crossing fibers
The stimulated leg withdraws but the other does not extend, so balance is lost
cards.explanation: The withdrawal limb of the response is entirely ipsilateral and survives, but the supporting extension on the other side depends on crossing fibers, so weight shifts to a limb that has not stiffened. The ipsilateral arc is intact, so a complete absence of response is not possible. Nothing in this lesion reverses the flexor and extensor assignments. Bilateral extension would require excitation of extensors on the stimulated side, which is actively inhibited.

cards.q: Why does a painful stimulus to the hand of a seated person produce a different overall pattern than the same stimulus to the foot of a standing person?
cards.a: Crossed extension supports body weight, so it is prominent in the leg and minimal in the seated arm.
options: The arm withdrawal reflex is monosynaptic while the leg withdrawal reflex is polysynaptic
The arm has few nociceptors, so the response there is largely voluntary rather than reflex
Crossed extension supports body weight, so it is prominent in the leg and minimal in the seated arm
Painful signals from the hand are integrated in the brainstem rather than in the spinal cord itself
cards.explanation: Both stimuli produce ipsilateral flexor withdrawal, but the crossed extension that preserves balance is only useful when the body weight must be transferred, which is the standing situation. The hand is densely supplied with nociceptors, so the first distractor fails at the premise. Both withdrawal reflexes are polysynaptic. Integration of both is spinal, with the brain informed afterward through ascending pathways.

cards.q: A withdrawal reflex is elicited with a stimulus lasting only 5 ms, yet the limb stays flexed for nearly a second. What best explains the prolonged contraction, and why does the patellar reflex not behave this way?
cards.a: Afterdischarge from reverberating interneuron circuits, which a monosynaptic arc does not have.
options: Slow conduction in the afferent and efferent fibers, which the patellar reflex does not have
Afterdischarge from reverberating interneuron circuits, which a monosynaptic arc does not have
Continued transmitter release at the neuromuscular junction, which the patellar reflex lacks
Prolonged receptor potentials in nociceptors combined with unusually slow flexor muscle fibers
cards.explanation: Once interneuron chains and loops are excited, they keep re-exciting the motor pool after the afferent volley has passed, and the multi-segmental spread keeps many motor neurons involved, so flexion outlasts the stimulus by orders of magnitude. Slow conduction shifts the start of the response by milliseconds and cannot stretch it to a second. Receptor potentials and muscle twitch duration are also far too brief to account for it. Neuromuscular transmission works the same way in both reflexes and stops when motor neuron firing stops.

cards.q: What information does the dorsal column pathway carry?
cards.a: Fine touch, vibration, and conscious proprioception.
options: Fine touch, vibration, and conscious proprioception
Unconscious proprioception bound for the cerebellum
Voluntary motor commands to skeletal muscle
Pain, temperature, and crude touch
cards.explanation: The dorsal columns carry the discriminative senses, the ones that need precise timing and a small receptive field, which is why vibration and joint position travel here. Pain and temperature ascend in the spinothalamic pathway instead. Voluntary motor commands descend in the corticospinal tract, so they move the opposite direction. Crude touch is largely a spinothalamic function, and confining the dorsal columns to it leaves vibration and proprioception unaccounted for.

cards.q: What information does the spinothalamic pathway carry?
cards.a: Pain and temperature.
options: Conscious proprioception from muscles and joints
Voluntary motor commands to skeletal muscle
Fine touch and vibration
Pain and temperature
cards.explanation: Spinothalamic fibers arise from dorsal horn neurons that receive small pain and temperature afferents, so this is the route by which a burn or a pinprick reaches consciousness. Fine touch and vibration travel in the dorsal columns. Conscious proprioception also uses the dorsal columns. Motor commands descend rather than ascend and belong to the corticospinal tract.

cards.q: What does the corticospinal tract carry?
cards.a: Voluntary motor commands from the cortex to spinal motor neurons.
options: Autonomic commands to smooth muscle and glands
Voluntary motor commands from the cortex to spinal motor neurons
Proprioceptive information from muscle spindles to the cerebellum
Pain and temperature from the body up to the cortex
cards.explanation: The corticospinal tract is the main descending pathway for skilled voluntary movement, running from motor cortex to the ventral horn motor neurons that drive skeletal muscle. Pain and temperature ascend in the spinothalamic pathway. Unconscious proprioception to the cerebellum travels in the spinocerebellar tracts. Autonomic output leaves through preganglionic fibers of the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions, not the corticospinal tract.

cards.q: Where does the dorsal column pathway cross the midline?
cards.a: In the medulla, at the nucleus gracilis and nucleus cuneatus.
options: In the midbrain, at the level of the cerebral peduncle
In the thalamus, at the ventral posterolateral nucleus
In the spinal cord, a segment or two above where the fibers enter
In the medulla, at the nucleus gracilis and nucleus cuneatus
cards.explanation: The first order fiber ascends on its own side to the nucleus gracilis or cuneatus in the medulla, and only the second order fiber crosses there before ascending as the medial lemniscus. Crossing within a segment or two of entry is the spinothalamic arrangement, and confusing the two is what reverses lesion patterns. No crossing happens in the midbrain for this pathway. The thalamus is the relay to cortex, not a crossing point.

cards.q: Where does the spinothalamic pathway cross the midline?
cards.a: In the spinal cord, a segment or two above where the fibers enter.
options: In the spinal cord, a segment or two above where the fibers enter
In the midbrain, just below the thalamic relay
In the medulla, where the internal arcuate fibers cross the midline
In the pons, at the level of the medial lemniscus
cards.explanation: The second order neuron in the dorsal horn sends its axon through the anterior white commissure to the other side almost immediately, then ascends contralaterally, which is why a cord lesion here causes a deficit on the opposite side. Crossing in the medulla describes the dorsal column pathway. Nothing crosses in the pons for this pathway. A pathway that never crossed could not deliver body sensation to the opposite hemisphere.

cards.q: Where does the lateral corticospinal tract cross the midline?
cards.a: At the pyramids of the medulla.
options: At the spinal cord segment where its fibers end
In the midbrain at the cerebral peduncles
At the pyramids of the medulla
In the internal capsule
cards.explanation: About 90 percent of corticospinal fibers cross at the pyramidal decussation in the caudal medulla and then descend in the lateral column of the cord on the side they will control. Crossing at the target segment is not how the lateral tract is organized. The internal capsule and the cerebral peduncle are places these fibers pass through on the same side as the cortex that sent them, not places where they cross.

cards.q: Where are the cell bodies of the second order neurons of the spinothalamic pathway?
cards.a: In the dorsal horn of the cord, near the level of entry.
options: In the ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus
In the dorsal root ganglion beside the spinal cord
In the dorsal horn of the cord, near the level of entry
In the nucleus gracilis or cuneatus of the medulla
cards.explanation: Pain and temperature afferents synapse in the dorsal horn, and it is that dorsal horn neuron whose axon crosses and ascends, which is why the crossing happens so low. The dorsal root ganglion holds the first order cell body. The nucleus gracilis holds the second order cell body of the dorsal column pathway. The thalamic nucleus holds the third order neuron for both sensory pathways.

cards.q: Which thalamic nucleus relays both dorsal column and spinothalamic input to the cerebral cortex?
cards.a: The ventral posterolateral nucleus.
options: The lateral geniculate nucleus
The ventral posterolateral nucleus
The medial geniculate nucleus
The anterior nucleus
cards.explanation: Both body sensory pathways converge on the ventral posterolateral nucleus, whose third order neurons project to the somatosensory cortex. The lateral geniculate nucleus is the visual relay. The medial geniculate nucleus is the auditory relay. The anterior nucleus belongs to limbic circuitry and carries no somatosensory relay function.

cards.q: The dorsal column on the left side of the spinal cord is damaged at T6. Where is vibration sense lost?
cards.a: On the left side of the body below T6.
options: On both sides of the body below T6
On the left side of the body above T6
On the right side of the body below T6
On the left side of the body below T6
cards.explanation: Dorsal column fibers ascend on the same side they entered and do not cross until the medulla, so a lesion in the cord takes out sensation from the same side, below the level of the injury. A contralateral deficit would require the fibers to have crossed already, which happens only above the medulla. Segments above the lesion send their fibers into the column above the damage, so they are unaffected. A bilateral loss would require damage to both columns.

cards.q: The spinothalamic tract on the right side of the spinal cord is cut at T10. Where is pain and temperature sensation lost?
cards.a: On the left side of the body below the level of the lesion.
options: On the left side of the body below the level of the lesion
On the left side of the body above the level of the lesion
On both sides of the body at the level of the lesion only
On the right side of the body below the level of the lesion
cards.explanation: These fibers cross within a segment or two of entering the cord, so the right side tract is already carrying signals that came from the left side of the body, and cutting it removes left sided pain and temperature below the injury. An ipsilateral deficit would be expected only if the pathway crossed higher up, as the dorsal columns do. Levels above the lesion enter the tract above the damage. A deficit confined to the level of the lesion describes damage to the crossing fibers themselves rather than the ascending tract.

cards.q: The lateral corticospinal tract is damaged on the left side of the spinal cord at C7. Which side of the body is weak?
cards.a: The left side, below the level of the lesion.
options: The left side, above the level of the lesion
The left side, below the level of the lesion
Both sides equally
The right side, below the level of the lesion
cards.explanation: These fibers crossed at the pyramids in the medulla, well above the cord, so by the time they reach C7 they are on the same side as the muscles they control and the weakness is ipsilateral to the cord lesion. A contralateral weakness would require the crossing to happen below C7, which it does not. Segments above the lesion receive their descending fibers before the damage. A bilateral deficit would require both lateral columns to be involved.

cards.q: A stroke damages corticospinal fibers in the right internal capsule, above the pyramids. Which side of the body is weak?
cards.a: The left side of the body.
options: The left side of the body
The right side of the body
Neither side, because the fibers have not yet crossed
Both sides of the body equally
cards.explanation: The internal capsule lies above the pyramidal decussation, so fibers there still have their crossing ahead of them and control the opposite side of the body, giving a contralateral weakness. An ipsilateral weakness would be the answer for a lesion in the cord, below the crossing. A single sided capsular lesion cannot weaken both sides. The fact that the fibers have not yet crossed is exactly why the deficit appears on the other side, not why it is absent.

cards.q: A patient has lost pain and temperature sensation in the right leg but has normal vibration sense there. Which tract on which side is damaged?
cards.a: The left spinothalamic tract.
options: The left dorsal column
The right spinothalamic tract
The right dorsal column
The left spinothalamic tract
cards.explanation: Signals from the right leg cross low in the cord and ascend in the left spinothalamic tract, so that is the tract carrying the lost information. The right spinothalamic tract carries the left side of the body. Either dorsal column would produce a vibration deficit, and vibration is preserved here, so the dorsal columns can be excluded on the pattern of loss alone.

cards.q: The medial lemniscus is damaged on the right side of the pons. Where is fine touch and vibration lost?
cards.a: On the left side of the body.
options: Only on the right side of the face
On both sides of the body
On the left side of the body
On the right side of the body
cards.explanation: The medial lemniscus forms after the dorsal column fibers have already crossed in the medulla, so a lesion above that point, such as in the pons, produces a contralateral deficit. An ipsilateral deficit would be expected only for a lesion below the crossing, in the cord. A one sided lesion cannot affect both sides. Facial sensation travels with the trigeminal system, so a body pathway lesion does not confine itself to the face.

cards.q: Why does a spinothalamic lesion produce a sensory level a segment or two below the level of the injury rather than exactly at it?
cards.a: Fibers ascend a segment or two before crossing, so those entering just below the lesion escape it.
options: Pain fibers cross in the medulla, well above the injury, so the level shifts downward
Fibers ascend a segment or two before crossing, so those entering just below the lesion escape it
The dorsal columns take over pain sensation for the top two segments below the lesion
Pain fibers conduct slowly, so the sensory deficit appears to lag behind the level of the injury
cards.explanation: Because the crossing is delayed by a segment or two, the fibers from dermatomes immediately below the lesion have already passed the damaged level on the other side, so the loss begins slightly lower than the injury. Conduction velocity has nothing to do with where a deficit appears on the body. The dorsal columns carry different modalities and cannot substitute for pain and temperature. Crossing in the medulla is the dorsal column arrangement, and if it applied here the deficit would be ipsilateral instead.

cards.q: The spinal cord is hemisected on the left at T10. Predict the pattern of deficits below the lesion.
cards.a: Weakness and loss of vibration and position sense on the left, with pain and temperature loss on the right.
options: Weakness and loss of vibration and position sense on the right, with pain and temperature loss on the left
Loss of all sensation and of all strength on the left side only, with the right side normal
Weakness and loss of vibration and position sense on the left, with pain and temperature loss on the right
Weakness on the left together with loss of pain, temperature, and vibration all on the left
cards.explanation: Two of the three tracts cross above the lesion, so corticospinal weakness and dorsal column loss appear on the same side as the cut, while the spinothalamic tract crossed low and its loss appears on the opposite side, beginning a segment or two down. Reversing the sides swaps the crossed and uncrossed pathways. Losing everything on one side ignores that pain and temperature have already changed sides. Placing all deficits on the left leaves the low crossing of the spinothalamic tract unaccounted for.

cards.q: A patient has weakness and loss of vibration sense in the right leg and loss of pain and temperature in the left leg, all below the level of the umbilicus. Where is the lesion?
cards.a: A hemisection of the right side of the cord at about T10.
options: A hemisection of the right side of the cord at about T10
A hemisection of the left side of the cord at about T10
A complete transection of the cord at T10
A lesion of the right internal capsule
cards.explanation: Motor and dorsal column deficits mark the side of a cord lesion because those tracts cross above it, so right sided weakness and right sided vibration loss place the injury on the right, and the crossed spinothalamic loss on the left confirms it. A left sided hemisection would give the mirror image of this pattern. An internal capsule lesion would produce weakness and sensory loss all on one side of the body, and would not spare the arm and trunk in this way. A complete transection would abolish everything on both sides below the level.

cards.q: A cavity expands in the center of the cervical cord and interrupts the fibers crossing in the anterior white commissure at C5 to T1. Predict the sensory findings in the arms.
cards.a: Loss of pain and temperature in both arms with vibration and position sense preserved.
options: Loss of all sensation in one arm only
Loss of pain and temperature in both legs with the arms spared
Loss of vibration and position sense in both arms with pain and temperature preserved
Loss of pain and temperature in both arms with vibration and position sense preserved
cards.explanation: The crossing fibers of the spinothalamic pathway pass through the center of the cord, so a central cavity interrupts them bilaterally at those segments, while the dorsal columns sit posteriorly and are spared, producing a split pattern of loss. Losing vibration instead would require damage to the dorsal columns, which the cavity has not reached. A one sided total loss would require a hemisection rather than a central lesion. The legs are supplied by fibers that crossed lower down and are already ascending in the lateral column, so they escape.

cards.q: A patient has weakness of the right arm and leg. If the lesion is in the spinal cord, which side is it on, and if the lesion is in the motor cortex, which side is it on?
cards.a: The right side of the cord, or the left side of the cortex.
options: The right side of the cord, or the left side of the cortex
The left side of the cord, or the right side of the cortex
The right side in both locations
The left side in both locations
cards.explanation: The pyramidal decussation is the dividing line: below it, in the cord, the fibers already serve the same side, so a cord lesion is ipsilateral to the weakness, while above it, in the cortex, the fibers have not crossed yet, so a cortical lesion is contralateral. Reversing both answers puts the decussation in the wrong place. Choosing the same side in both locations ignores the crossing entirely, which is the single most common error in reading these patterns.

cards.q: Where is cerebrospinal fluid produced?
cards.a: At the choroid plexus in the ventricles.
options: By the pia mater covering the cortex
At the choroid plexus in the ventricles
At the arachnoid granulations
By the endothelium of the dural venous sinuses
cards.explanation: Choroid plexus epithelium actively secretes CSF into the ventricles at roughly 500 mL per day. Arachnoid granulations are where the fluid is absorbed, the opposite end of the circuit. The pia is a thin covering membrane and does not secrete the fluid. The dural venous sinuses receive CSF rather than make it.

cards.q: Which of these is a function of cerebrospinal fluid?
cards.a: It supports the brain so that its effective weight is greatly reduced.
