options: It establishes the resting membrane potential of central neurons
It supplies the main metabolic fuel used by neurons in the cortex
It delivers oxygen to neurons in place of the cerebral blood supply
It supports the brain so that its effective weight is greatly reduced
cards.explanation: Floating in CSF reduces the effective weight of the brain from about 1400 g to roughly 50 g, which protects the base of the brain and its vessels from being crushed. Oxygen is delivered by blood through cerebral capillaries, not by CSF. Resting membrane potential is set by ion gradients and membrane permeability at each cell. Glucose is the fuel and arrives through the blood, although CSF composition does help keep the neuronal environment stable.

cards.q: Where does cerebrospinal fluid return to the blood?
cards.a: At the arachnoid granulations projecting into the dural sinuses.
options: Across the blood brain barrier into the brain capillaries
At the capillary beds of the choroid plexus in the ventricles
At the arachnoid granulations projecting into the dural sinuses
Through lymphatic vessels running within the pia mater
cards.explanation: Arachnoid granulations act as one way valves that let CSF pass into venous blood once CSF pressure exceeds venous pressure. Choroid plexus capillaries supply the fluid that becomes CSF, so flow there runs the other way. The blood brain barrier restricts movement between blood and brain tissue and is not the bulk drainage route. Classic lymphatic vessels do not run in the pia.

cards.q: About how much cerebrospinal fluid is present in an adult at any one time?
cards.a: About 150 mL.
options: About 1500 mL
About 15 mL
About 150 mL
About 500 mL
cards.explanation: Roughly 150 mL circulates at any moment, and since about 500 mL is produced each day the whole volume is replaced several times over. About 15 mL is far too small to fill the ventricles and subarachnoid space. About 500 mL is the daily production, a value students often mistake for the standing volume. About 1500 mL is closer to the mass of the brain itself in grams.

cards.q: What structure forms the blood brain barrier?
cards.a: Tight junctions between the endothelial cells of brain capillaries.
options: The thin layer of cerebrospinal fluid surrounding each neuron
Tight junctions between the endothelial cells of brain capillaries
Fenestrations in the endothelium of the brain capillary wall
The pia mater covering the entire outer surface of the brain
cards.explanation: Brain capillary endothelial cells are sealed to one another by continuous tight junctions, and astrocyte end feet wrap the vessel and help induce and maintain those junctions, so anything entering must pass through the cells rather than between them. Fenestrations are pores that make a capillary leaky, the opposite arrangement, and they are found in tissues such as the kidney glomerulus. The pia is a covering membrane, not a diffusion barrier at the capillary. CSF bathes the outside of the brain and ventricles and does not form the barrier.

cards.q: Which property allows a substance to cross the blood brain barrier most easily by simple diffusion?
cards.a: High lipid solubility.
options: High lipid solubility
A strong net electrical charge
Tight binding to plasma albumin
Large molecular size
cards.explanation: With the paracellular route sealed, a molecule must dissolve into and pass through the endothelial cell membranes, and lipid solubility is exactly what allows that, which is why anesthetics and alcohol enter the brain within seconds. Large molecules cross poorly regardless of other properties. A charged molecule cannot enter a lipid bilayer without a transporter. A drug bound to albumin is held in the plasma and only its free fraction is available to cross.

cards.q: How does glucose cross the blood brain barrier?
cards.a: By carrier mediated transport using GLUT1.
options: Through fenestrations between endothelial cells
By simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer
By vesicular pinocytosis across the endothelial cell
By carrier mediated transport using GLUT1
cards.explanation: Glucose is polar and cannot pass through the membrane on its own, so the endothelium expresses abundant GLUT1 to carry it down its concentration gradient into the brain. Simple diffusion is the route for lipid soluble molecules only. Brain capillaries have no fenestrations, which is the whole point of the barrier. Pinocytosis is markedly limited in these endothelial cells, unlike in capillaries elsewhere.

cards.q: How does the composition of cerebrospinal fluid compare with that of blood plasma?
cards.a: CSF contains far less protein.
options: CSF contains far more protein
CSF contains far less protein
CSF contains far more potassium
CSF and plasma have essentially identical composition
cards.explanation: CSF is a secreted fluid rather than a filtrate, so protein content is a small fraction of the plasma value, and K+ is also held slightly lower and more tightly regulated to keep neuronal excitability stable. High protein in CSF is an abnormal finding, not the normal state. High K+ in CSF would destabilize resting membrane potentials in neurons. Identical composition would defeat the purpose of a regulated extracellular environment.

cards.q: Two drugs act equally well at the same brain receptor. Drug A is highly lipid soluble and drug B is fully ionized at body pH. Which reaches the brain better?
cards.a: Drug A, because lipid soluble molecules diffuse through the endothelial membranes.
options: Drug A, because lipid soluble molecules diffuse through the endothelial membranes
Both equally, because the barrier excludes only large molecules
Drug B, because charged molecules are pulled across by the membrane potential
Neither, because every drug requires a specific transporter
cards.explanation: The barrier forces a transcellular route, so the ability to dissolve in membrane lipid decides passive entry and the lipid soluble drug wins easily. The small membrane potential across an endothelial cell cannot drag an ion through a lipid bilayer that offers it no path. Size matters, but charge and lipid solubility matter at least as much, so treating the barrier as a size filter is incomplete. Some substances do use transporters, but many drugs cross by simple diffusion without one.

cards.q: Dopamine given intravenously does not reach the brain, but L-dopa does. Why?
cards.a: L-dopa is carried by an amino acid transporter that dopamine cannot use.
options: L-dopa dissolves in cerebrospinal fluid far better than dopamine does
L-dopa is smaller than dopamine and slips between the endothelial cells
L-dopa is carried by an amino acid transporter that dopamine cannot use
Dopamine is destroyed by the choroid plexus before it reaches brain tissue
cards.explanation: L-dopa is an amino acid and is recognized by the large neutral amino acid carrier in the endothelial membrane, giving it a route that polar dopamine simply does not have. Nothing slips between the endothelial cells, since tight junctions seal that path for both molecules. Choroid plexus destruction is not the limiting step, as the barrier blocks dopamine at the capillary. Both molecules are water soluble, so solubility in CSF is not what separates them.

cards.q: The cerebral aqueduct becomes blocked. Predict what happens.
cards.a: CSF accumulates above the block and pressure rises in the ventricles.
options: CSF is rerouted through the arachnoid granulations with no change in pressure
CSF drains into the spinal canal and the brain shrinks
CSF production stops at once, so pressure falls
CSF accumulates above the block and pressure rises in the ventricles
cards.explanation: Choroid plexus secretion continues largely independent of pressure, so fluid keeps entering the ventricles upstream of the block while it can no longer reach the absorption sites, and the ventricles distend. Production does not shut off promptly when pressure rises, which is why obstruction is dangerous. Reaching the granulations requires passing the block, so no rerouting is available. Drainage downward is also blocked, so the brain tissue is compressed rather than allowed to shrink.

cards.q: A brain weighing about 1400 g in air presses on the floor of the skull with an effective weight of only about 50 g. What accounts for this?
cards.a: It floats in cerebrospinal fluid, which provides buoyancy.
options: The dura suspends the entire brain from the roof of the skull
It floats in cerebrospinal fluid, which provides buoyancy
Brain tissue is less dense than any fluid that surrounds it
The blood brain barrier holds the brain in position
cards.explanation: Because brain tissue and CSF have nearly the same density, the fluid supports almost the whole weight of the organ, which is why a brain removed from CSF deforms under its own mass. Dural folds do help stabilize the brain, but they do not carry its weight. The blood brain barrier controls chemical exchange and has no mechanical role. Brain tissue is very slightly denser than CSF, not less dense, so it does not simply float free.

cards.q: Which region of the brain can respond to blood borne hormones and toxins despite the blood brain barrier?
cards.a: The circumventricular organs, where the capillaries are leaky.
options: The internal capsule, which contains no capillaries at all
The choroid plexus epithelium, which lacks tight junctions
The primary somatosensory cortex, which expresses extra transporters
The circumventricular organs, where the capillaries are leaky
cards.explanation: A few small regions bordering the ventricles, including the area postrema and parts of the hypothalamus, have fenestrated capillaries so the brain can sample the blood directly, which is how a vomiting reflex to circulating toxins is possible. The somatosensory cortex has an ordinary barrier and no special sampling role. Every region of the brain, including white matter tracts, is supplied by capillaries. The choroid plexus epithelium does have tight junctions, which is what makes it a blood to CSF barrier.

cards.q: A drug is 99 percent bound to plasma albumin. What is the effect on its entry into the brain?
cards.a: Entry is limited, because only the free fraction is available to cross.
options: Entry is limited, because only the free fraction is available to cross
Entry is increased, because albumin is carried across along with it
Entry is prevented completely, because bound drug is chemically inactive
Entry is unaffected, because protein binding occurs only in the liver
cards.explanation: Only unbound drug can diffuse or be transported across the endothelium, so heavy protein binding leaves a small free concentration to drive entry and slows the rise of drug levels in the brain. Albumin itself is far too large to cross the barrier, so it cannot ferry the drug in. Binding happens in the plasma throughout the circulation, not only in the liver. Entry is reduced rather than abolished, since bound and free drug are in equilibrium and free drug is continuously replaced as it leaves.

cards.q: Meningitis inflames the meninges and loosens the endothelial tight junctions. Predict the effect on an antibiotic that normally penetrates the brain poorly.
cards.a: More antibiotic reaches the CSF while inflammation lasts, then less as it resolves.
options: The antibiotic becomes trapped in the CSF and cannot return to the bloodstream
Penetration is unchanged, because the barrier depends only on lipid solubility
More antibiotic reaches the CSF while inflammation lasts, then less as it resolves
Less antibiotic reaches the CSF, because inflammation blocks the brain capillaries
cards.explanation: The barrier is a property of the junctions, so loosening them opens a paracellular route and raises drug entry, and the effect fades as the junctions reseal. Inflammation increases permeability rather than blocking flow. Lipid solubility governs the transcellular route but does not make the paracellular route irrelevant, so penetration is not fixed. Movement across a leaky barrier works in both directions, so trapping does not occur.

cards.q: The arachnoid granulations are scarred after a hemorrhage while the choroid plexus continues to secrete at its normal rate. Predict what happens over the following days.
cards.a: CSF volume and pressure rise, because production continues while absorption falls.
options: CSF volume falls, because secretion shuts down as soon as the pressure rises
Nothing changes, because production and absorption are independent of one another
CSF volume and pressure rise, because production continues while absorption falls
CSF is absorbed across the blood brain barrier instead, at exactly the same rate
cards.explanation: CSF volume is set by the balance of a nearly constant secretion rate against a pressure dependent absorption rate, so damaging absorption while secretion continues drives volume and pressure upward. Secretion is not strongly suppressed by rising pressure, which is exactly why the imbalance persists. The two processes are linked through volume, so they cannot be treated as independent. The blood brain barrier is not a bulk drainage route and cannot substitute for the granulations.

cards.q: Three substances are presented to the blood brain barrier: a small lipid soluble anesthetic, the amino acid phenylalanine, and a large plasma protein. Which crosses most readily and which least?
cards.a: The anesthetic crosses most readily and the plasma protein least.
options: The plasma protein crosses most readily and the anesthetic least
All three cross at similar rates, because the barrier is only a size filter
Phenylalanine crosses most readily and the anesthetic least
The anesthetic crosses most readily and the plasma protein least
cards.explanation: A small lipid soluble molecule dissolves straight through the endothelial membranes with no carrier needed, phenylalanine has a carrier but is limited by how many transporters are available, and a large protein has neither route open to it. Ranking the protein first inverts every property that matters. Carrier mediated entry is real but slower and saturable, so it does not outrun free diffusion of a lipid soluble drug. Treating the barrier as a size filter ignores lipid solubility and transporters, the two factors doing most of the work.

cards.q: Mannitol, which cannot cross the blood brain barrier, is infused into the blood. Predict the effect on brain water.
cards.a: Water moves from brain tissue into the blood, because plasma osmolarity rises.
options: Water moves from brain tissue into the blood, because plasma osmolarity rises
Water moves into the brain, because mannitol drags fluid across the barrier with it
The brain swells, because mannitol is taken up and converted to glucose by neurons
Nothing changes, because water cannot cross the barrier any better than mannitol
cards.explanation: A solute that stays in the plasma is an effective osmole across that barrier, so it raises the osmotic pressure of blood relative to brain tissue and pulls water out, lowering brain volume. Mannitol cannot drag water into a compartment it never enters. Water crosses the barrier freely even though mannitol does not, which is precisely what makes the osmotic effect possible. Mannitol is not metabolized to glucose by neurons.

cards.q: On the standard deep tendon reflex scale, which grade is recorded for a normal response?
cards.explanation: The scale runs from 0 to 4+, and 2+ is the expected brisk but not exaggerated response. A grade of 0 means no response at all even with reinforcement. A grade of 1+ means present but diminished, which is below normal though not always abnormal. A grade of 4+ means very brisk with clonus and points to loss of descending inhibition.

cards.q: What does a deep tendon reflex graded 4+ mean?
cards.a: A very brisk response accompanied by clonus.
options: No response even with reinforcement
A normal, expected response
A very brisk response accompanied by clonus
A response that appears only with reinforcement
cards.explanation: A 4+ grade is the top of the scale and describes a hyperactive reflex with repetitive beats of clonus, which suggests an upper motor neuron problem. The normal response is 2+. A response requiring reinforcement is graded 1+ or is recorded with the reinforcement noted. No response at all is graded 0.

cards.q: Which spinal segments does the patellar reflex test?
cards.a: L2 to L4.
options: L2 to L4
S1 and S2
T10 to T12
C5 and C6
cards.explanation: The quadriceps and its femoral nerve supply arise from L2 to L4, so a normal knee jerk tests the integrity of that arc. S1 is the ankle jerk. C5 and C6 give the biceps reflex. The T10 to T12 segments supply abdominal wall muscles and have no tendon jerk of this kind.

cards.q: Which spinal segment does the Achilles, or ankle jerk, reflex test?
options: S1
L4
C7
cards.explanation: The gastrocnemius and soleus draw their supply mainly from S1, so the ankle jerk is the standard test of that segment. L4 contributes to the knee jerk instead. C7 is tested by the triceps reflex. T12 supplies trunk musculature and no standard tendon jerk.

cards.q: Which deep tendon reflex tests the C5 and C6 segments?
cards.a: The biceps reflex.
options: The triceps reflex
The patellar reflex
The Achilles reflex
The biceps reflex
cards.explanation: The biceps and its musculocutaneous nerve supply come from C5 and C6, so tapping the biceps tendon tests those roots. The triceps reflex tests C7. The patellar reflex tests L2 to L4. The Achilles reflex tests S1.

cards.q: What is the purpose of the Jendrassik maneuver during reflex testing?
cards.a: To reinforce a weak reflex so that it can be judged fairly.
options: To measure the latency of the reflex response accurately
To test the voluntary strength of the muscle being tapped
To reinforce a weak reflex so that it can be judged fairly
To relax the subject so that the reflex disappears entirely
cards.explanation: Having the subject pull interlocked fingers apart raises the background excitability of the motor pool in the leg, so a reflex that looked absent may appear, which prevents recording a false 0. It increases rather than suppresses the response. It provides no timing information, so latency must be measured some other way. It tests neither the strength nor the effort of the muscle being tapped.

cards.q: About how long is the latency of the patellar reflex, from tendon tap to the start of contraction?
cards.a: About 20 to 40 ms.
options: About 20 to 40 ms
About 150 to 250 ms
About 1 to 2 s
About 1 to 2 ms
cards.explanation: Conduction up and down the leg plus one synaptic delay adds up to a few tens of milliseconds, which is the signature of a monosynaptic spinal arc. One to two milliseconds is about the cost of a single synapse and far too short for the round trip. About 150 to 250 ms is the range of a simple voluntary reaction time. One to two seconds is longer than any reflex or voluntary reaction.

cards.q: What does the ruler drop test measure?
cards.a: Voluntary reaction time.
options: The latency of the patellar reflex
Nerve conduction velocity in the forearm
The maximum force of a muscle contraction
Voluntary reaction time
cards.explanation: The subject must see the ruler fall, decide to close the hand, and execute the movement, so the distance the ruler falls converts into a reaction time that includes central processing. A tendon reflex latency is an order of magnitude shorter and cannot be captured this way. The test records timing, not force. Conduction velocity requires stimulating a nerve at two points and comparing latencies.

cards.q: A ruler is caught after falling 20 cm. Using d equal to one half g t squared, with g of 9.8 m/s squared, what is the reaction time?
cards.a: About 0.20 s.
options: About 0.45 s
About 0.20 s
About 0.02 s
About 2.0 s
cards.explanation: Rearranging gives t equal to the square root of two times 0.20 m divided by 9.8, which is the square root of about 0.041, or roughly 0.20 s, a typical simple reaction time. About 0.02 s would be shorter than a spinal reflex latency and is physically impossible for a visual response. About 0.45 s corresponds to a drop of roughly a meter. About 2.0 s is off by a factor of ten and would require a fall of nearly 20 m.

cards.q: A subject responds to a stimulus with a measured latency of 180 ms. Is this a reflex or a voluntary response?
cards.a: Voluntary, because 180 ms is far longer than a spinal reflex latency.
options: Voluntary, because 180 ms is far longer than a spinal reflex latency
Reflex, because voluntary responses always take less than 100 ms
Reflex, because spinal reflexes take about 200 ms
It cannot be decided, because latency says nothing about the pathway
cards.explanation: A monosynaptic spinal arc takes a few tens of milliseconds, so any response near 180 ms has spent time in cortical processing and must involve more than the cord. Placing spinal reflex latency near 200 ms confuses it with voluntary reaction time. Voluntary responses are the slower of the two, not the faster, so the third option has the comparison backwards. Latency is in fact the most useful single measurement for separating the two, because pathway length and synapse count determine it.

cards.q: A patient has an absent ankle jerk while the knee jerk is a normal 2+. What does this pattern suggest?
cards.a: A problem in the S1 reflex arc.
options: A normal variant that carries no localizing information
An upper motor neuron lesion above the lumbar segments
A problem in the S1 reflex arc
A problem in the L2 to L4 reflex arc
cards.explanation: Each tendon jerk tests a defined segment, so an isolated loss at the ankle with a normal knee jerk points at S1 and spares L2 to L4. A problem at L2 to L4 would show up as a diminished knee jerk instead. An upper motor neuron lesion removes descending inhibition and makes reflexes brisker, not absent. The pattern is segmental and therefore localizing, which is the reason reflexes are tested at several levels.

cards.q: On examination the leg reflexes are 4+ with clonus while the arm reflexes are 2+. What does this pattern suggest?
cards.a: An upper motor neuron lesion in the cord below the cervical segments.
options: A muscle disease that weakens the leg muscles selectively
Normal variation in an athlete with well trained legs
A peripheral nerve injury affecting the nerves supplying both legs
An upper motor neuron lesion in the cord below the cervical segments
cards.explanation: Loss of descending inhibition releases the spinal arcs below the lesion, so reflexes are exaggerated below it and normal above it, which places the injury between the cervical and lumbar levels. Peripheral nerve injury damages the arc itself and reduces or abolishes reflexes. Muscle disease weakens the effector and gives normal or reduced reflexes. Training does not produce clonus, which is always a released reflex.

cards.q: A reflex appears absent on repeated testing. What should be tried before recording it as 0?
cards.a: Reinforcement with the Jendrassik maneuver.
options: Testing the opposite limb and recording that value instead
Reinforcement with the Jendrassik maneuver
Tapping the muscle belly instead of the tendon
Asking the subject to contract the muscle during the tap
cards.explanation: Reinforcement raises motor pool excitability and often brings out a reflex that a tense or inattentive subject was suppressing, so it must be tried before recording a grade of 0. Tapping the muscle belly stretches the fibers differently and does not give a standard tendon jerk. A voluntary contraction during the tap contaminates the response and makes the reflex impossible to grade. The opposite limb is worth comparing but cannot substitute for the value on the side being tested.

cards.q: Why is a choice reaction time longer than a simple reaction time?
cards.a: The added decision step requires more central processing time.
options: Nerve fibers conduct more slowly when two choices are present
The receptor needs longer to detect a stimulus when there are two of them
The added decision step requires more central processing time
The muscle takes longer to contract for a chosen movement
cards.explanation: Both tasks share the same conduction and contraction times, so the extra 100 ms or so of a choice task comes from selecting between responses in the brain. Conduction velocity is fixed by fiber diameter and myelination and does not depend on the task. Contraction time is a property of the muscle and is unchanged. Receptor transduction takes the same few milliseconds regardless of how many stimuli might appear.

cards.q: Reaction time to a sound is usually a little shorter than reaction time to a light. What accounts for this?
cards.a: Auditory transduction and relay take less time than visual phototransduction.
options: Auditory responses are spinal reflexes while visual ones require cortex
Auditory transduction and relay take less time than visual phototransduction
Sound travels to the receptor faster than light travels to the eye
Auditory nerve fibers are unmyelinated and therefore conduct faster
cards.explanation: Hair cells transduce sound almost mechanically and the auditory pathway to motor output is short, while phototransduction involves a slower biochemical cascade in the retina, so the auditory route wins by tens of milliseconds. Light travels far faster than sound, so the first distractor reverses physics. Unmyelinated fibers conduct more slowly, not faster. Neither response is a spinal reflex, since both take more than 100 ms and require the brain.

cards.q: A student records 25 ms between the tendon tap and the first quadriceps electrical activity. Explain why this cannot be a voluntary response.
cards.a: Cortical processing alone takes over 100 ms, so 25 ms allows only a spinal arc.
options: Voluntary contractions produce no muscle electrical activity that can be recorded
A delay of 25 ms is too long for any reflex, so the response must be voluntary
Voluntary responses are always slower than 25 ms because muscle contracts slowly
Cortical processing alone takes over 100 ms, so 25 ms allows only a spinal arc
cards.explanation: The measured value fits conduction up the leg, one synapse, and conduction back down, and nothing is left over for the ascending pathway, cortical decision, and descending command that a voluntary movement needs. Muscle contraction speed is not the limiting factor and is the same for both kinds of response. Voluntary contraction produces the same kind of muscle electrical activity, so it is recordable. Calling 25 ms too long for a reflex inverts the actual timing, since that is the expected monosynaptic value.

cards.q: A subject knows exactly when the ruler will be released and catches it after only 12 cm. Is this a valid measure of reaction time, and what should change?
cards.a: No, anticipation shortens the measured time, so the release must be unpredictable.
options: No, anticipation shortens the measured time, so the release must be unpredictable
No, because the ruler must fall at least 20 cm before the formula can apply
Yes, because the drop distance still converts to a valid time by the formula
Yes, and the shorter time shows the response has become a spinal reflex
cards.explanation: Reaction time is defined as the delay after an unexpected stimulus, so a subject who is timing the release is partly moving in advance and the number no longer measures processing time. The arithmetic still works, but a valid conversion of an invalid measurement is still invalid. The formula holds for any distance, so the 20 cm figure is not a requirement. A response driven by prediction is still a voluntary movement, not a spinal reflex, which would take a few tens of milliseconds.

cards.q: After a tendon tap, two bursts of muscle activity are recorded, one beginning at 30 ms and one at 160 ms. How should they be interpreted?
cards.a: The 30 ms burst is the spinal stretch reflex and the 160 ms burst is voluntary.
options: The 30 ms burst is the voluntary response and the 160 ms burst is the spinal reflex
The 160 ms burst is an electrical artifact and should be discarded from the record
The 30 ms burst is the spinal stretch reflex and the 160 ms burst is voluntary
Both are spinal reflexes, one monosynaptic and one polysynaptic in the same segment
cards.explanation: Latency identifies the pathway: a few tens of milliseconds fits a cord level arc, while well over 100 ms requires transmission to the brain and back. Reversing the assignment would demand cortical processing in 30 ms, which is not possible. An extra interneuron adds only about a millisecond, so a polysynaptic spinal arc cannot account for a 130 ms gap. Discarding the late burst throws away real data that is exactly what this experiment is designed to reveal.

cards.q: In lab, the patellar reflex is graded 3+ on the right and 2+ on the left, with every other reflex symmetric. What is the most defensible interpretation, and what should be done next?
cards.a: The asymmetry matters more than either grade, so retest both sides with identical technique.
options: The left side is the abnormal one, since a 2+ grade sits below the expected range
Grades from different sides cannot be compared, so this difference should be ignored
A 3+ grade is abnormal by itself, so the right leg most likely has a peripheral nerve injury
The asymmetry matters more than either grade, so retest both sides with identical technique
cards.explanation: Reflex grading is subjective and sensitive to limb position, subject tension, and the force of the tap, so a one grade difference is worth confirming before it is treated as real, and asymmetry rather than absolute grade is what carries information. A 3+ grade falls within the range seen in normal people, so it is not abnormal by itself, and a peripheral nerve injury would reduce a reflex rather than increase it. A 2+ grade is the normal value, so the left side needs no explanation. Side to side comparison is the most reliable part of the examination and should not be discarded.
